name: prototype
intent: Create new objects by cloning a configured prototypical instance through a common cloning interface, so that creation no longer depends on the concrete classes or on repeating their construction and configuration work.
problem: A family of objects is needed in many pre-configured variants, and copying an existing configured instance would be cheaper, simpler and more faithful than rebuilding it from scratch - while a client that holds only a base interface cannot copy the object at all, because it knows neither the concrete class nor its fields or invariants. The recurring trigger is 'the object I need already exists as a preset/archetype/fixture; give me an independent copy of it' rather than 'construct a new one from parameters'.
context: Applies when construction is expensive or laborious (parsing, I/O, warm-up, validation, dependency wiring), when product kinds are configured at run time and should be produced from existing exemplars instead of hard-coded classes, and when a copy must be made through a base interface or class hierarchy (polymorphic cloning). It is most valuable in languages where classes are not first-class objects and where a client cannot see an object's internal state to copy it field by field.
benefits: Clients create objects without naming concrete classes: one clone() call on the prototype interface preserves the dynamic type, so installing or removing product kinds needs no client change.

Configuration becomes data rather than subclasses: a family of presets and archetypes are ordinary instances that can be registered and replaced at run time (GoF: adding and removing products at run time).
Cloning skips expensive or error-prone reconstruction: warmed caches, parsed structures, validated configuration and pre-computed state simply carry over into the copy.
Removes dummy-subclass explosion: variants that differed only in constructor initialisation collapse into prototypical instances that are cloned and adjusted.

Copy logic stays inside the class, which has access to its own private state (GoF: objects of the same class can inspect each other's private fields) - clients never hand-copy fields and cannot get them wrong.
Works where classes are not first-class objects: the configured instance plays the role a class object would play in Smalltalk or Objective-C.
tradeoffs: Implementing the clone operation correctly is the hard part, not the client: it must decide per field what is copied, shared or deep-copied, and the default member-wise copies of most languages silently alias mutable substructures.
Cycles and shared references break naive recursive copying: without an identity map the clone loops forever or duplicates nodes that the original shared.

Cloning typically bypasses constructors (Object.clone, MemberwiseClone, allocate + initialize_copy), so validation, identity assignment, registration and dependency wiring performed there are not re-established on the copy.
The clone raises identity questions that construction did not: entity ids, caches, listeners, locks and resource handles are shared by default - each one needs an explicit copy-or-share decision.
Two creation paths (constructor and clone) must be kept consistent; a field added to the constructor and forgotten in the clone is a silent defect that surfaces far from the clone site.
The prototype registry, when used, is global mutable state: runtime registration brings lifetime, ownership and concurrency questions along with the flexibility.
It pays off only with many run-time-configured variants; for a handful of products the clone plus registry machinery is more indirection than a constructor, a copy-with-overrides call or a builder.
Deep copy is not automatically faster than construction: it allocates while walking the graph, and for cheap immutable configuration a direct construction can be the cheaper path.

Modern language alternatives (with-expressions, copy.replace, structuredClone) may make a dedicated clone interface unnecessary for simple cases; prefer language idioms before introducing the pattern.

participants.responsibility: Declares the interface for cloning itself (conventionally clone()/copy()), so clients can copy an object without knowing its concrete type.
Implements the cloning operation for its own state: creates a new instance of its dynamic type and decides per field what is copied, deep-copied or shared.
Creates new objects by asking a prototype to clone itself and then adjusting the copy, instead of instantiating concrete classes.
Optional: keeps named prototypical instances and hands out clones of a requested exemplar, so new kinds can be installed and removed without client changes.

use_cases: Document, diagram and music editors: a tool is parameterised with a prototypical graphic/note and creates new items by cloning it and adding the copy to the document (GoF's GraphicTool example).

Game engines and simulations: spawn units, projectiles or particles from configured archetypes/prefabs rather than constructing each instance from parameters. Game engines like Unity (Prototype component), Unreal (Archetypes), and Bevy (entity cloning) all embody this pattern natively.
Test-data construction: keep one fully configured fixture and clone it per test, so each test mutates its own independent copy.
Configuration presets: subscription plans, discount campaigns, device profiles, request contexts - clone the base preset and override a few fields.
Warm-up-sensitive structures: clone a prepared AST, parsed schema, compiled matrix or pre-populated cache instead of rebuilding it per consumer.
Multi-document/session state: copy a template workspace or session state and specialise the copy, keeping the template intact.
UI component libraries: spawn repeated UI elements (dialog boxes, form fields, menu items) from configured prototypes at runtime.
Workflow and business-process engines: clone a pre-configured workflow step or approval task template to instantiate process instances.

Unity editor workflows: Unity's PrefabUtility.InstantiatePrefab creates a new scene instance from a configured Prefab asset while retaining a live connection to the original, so the Prefab is an explicit editable prototype.

Unreal Engine object graphs: StaticDuplicateObject duplicates a source UObject and contained objects while remapping references to the duplicated copies, providing graph-aware cloning of configured archetypes without naming each concrete component.
Bevy ECS: EntityCloner can spawn a clone of an existing entity and select or override per-component clone behavior, making a configured entity an explicit runtime prototype.
avoid_when: Objects are small and cheap to construct: a constructor, a record/with-expression, a data-class copy or a builder is simpler and keeps one creation path.
The set of products is closed and known at compile time: plain constructors, an enum/variant plus pattern matching, or a parameter object is clearer than a registry of prototypes.
A copy-with-a-few-changed-fields call already exists in the language (with-expression, copy(), dataclasses.replace, case-class copy) - name that idiom instead of introducing a clone interface.
The graph holds non-copyable resources (sockets, file handles, locks, connection pools, thread-local state): model the resource separately; cloning would duplicate ownership, not state.
The type is genuinely immutable and cheap to share: sharing the instance (or a flyweight) is correct, and cloning only wastes memory.
Cloning is used to paper over missing immutability or missing value semantics instead of designing them.
anti_patterns: Serialization round-trip (JSON/reflection deep clone) presented as the cloning mechanism: it drops types, invariants, cycles and identity, and silently mangles dates/maps/undefined values.
A clone() that returns a shallow copy while callers assume deep independence - 'cloned' objects that share mutable state.
Building a full prototype registry for two or three products, or implementing clone() on classes where a copy constructor/with-expression already says it better.
Cloning mutable entities as a substitute for immutability or value semantics, spreading defensive copies across the codebase.
Deep-copying a graph that contains resources or observers: cloned locks, cloned connections, duplicated listener registrations.
A registry whose prototypes are mutable and shared: one client mutates the exemplar and every later clone inherits the change.
Relying on JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) for deep cloning: loses Date (becomes string), undefined, BigInt, Map, Set, RegExp, and throws on circular references.
design_principles: Program to an interface, not an implementation: clients call clone() on the prototype type and never name concrete product classes.
Delegation over inheritance: creation is delegated to the object being copied, so no parallel Creator hierarchy is needed (GoF: Prototype is creation through delegation).
Open/closed principle: new product kinds are installed by registering instances, without editing client code.
Single source of truth for configuration: presets and archetypes exist as instances, not as subclasses that differ only in constructor code.
Encapsulation: the class itself knows its internal structure, so copying respects private state instead of re-exposing it to clients.
Prefer immutability: immutable state and substructures can be shared safely between original and clone, shrinking the deep-copy surface.
Explicit over implicit: clone semantics (shallow/deep/mixed) must be documented and testable, never assumed.
best_practices: Decide and document per field whether the clone copies, deep-copies or shares it - make the depth explicit in the name (Clone vs DeepClone vs Copy) or in the contract, never implied.

Implement clone through a copy constructor or a generated copy (record with-expression, data-class copy(), derive(Clone), copy constructor) so construction stays in one place; hand-write deep clone only for graphs.
Preserve the dynamic type: call the superclass copy/super.clone() or construct the concrete type, and never let a clone() return a base-class instance for a subclass receiver.
Use an identity map / memo when copying object graphs so cycles terminate and shared references stay shared in the copy.
Re-initialise identity-bearing state (ids, timestamps, caches, registrations, listeners) after cloning; a clone must not silently inherit the original's identity.
Prefer typed, named copy methods (clone(): this, copy(), DeepClone(), with(preset)) over generic object-returning cloning in public APIs.
Treat prototype registry entries as immutable templates and synchronise or freeze registry updates if prototypes can be added at run time.
Validate clone independence with tests: mutate the clone's nested state and assert the original is unchanged; test cycles, shared references, and non-cloneable resources explicitly.

In language-idiomatic copying (Python copy.replace, JavaScript structuredClone, Rust Clone/Copy): use the native mechanism for simple cases and add a custom clone() only when polymorphic dispatch or special semantics are required.
Profile before committing to cloning: for cheap objects, constructor + field-overrides or a builder is simpler and faster than a clone with deep-copy machinery.
sources: Gamma, Helm, Johnson & Vlissides, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994) - Prototype, pp. 117-126 (creational patterns chapter: Clone operation, shallow vs deep copy, initializing clones).
